Common Atlantic grenadier Nezumia aequalis exhibits life-history traits characteristic of deep-water macrourids that experience low-energy environments and relatively stable thermal conditions. Field surveys conducted in the Northwest Atlantic indicate that females achieve sexual maturation, marked by the onset of gonadal recrudescence, at a total length of approximately 18.9 centimeters [Lp = approximately 18.9 centimeters]. This measurement distinguishes the species from several congeners that mature at smaller sizes, though it aligns broadly with patterns observed in other bathyal gadiforms inhabiting similar depths. The body mass recorded at this developmental stage, derived from length-weight regressions applied to trawl-caught specimens, corresponds to roughly 17.5 grams [Wwp = roughly 17.5 grams]. Such values reflect the slow growth and delayed reproductive scheduling that typify fishes residing in cold, food-limited benthic habitats.

Reproductive output in Nezumia aequalis has been quantified through histological examination of gravid ovaries obtained during seasonal research cruises. The maximum daily fecundity, derived from batch counts of hydrated oocytes, reaches approximately 29 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 29 eggs per day] under the prevailing thermal regime of 9.3 °C [T = 9.3 °C]. This rate is comparatively modest when placed alongside the prolific spawning strategies of shallow-water macrourids, suggesting an adaptive response to the energetic constraints of the deep continental slope. Adult females typically sustain this level of reproductive investment over a protracted spawning period, with multiple batches released across the breeding season. Such iteroparous scheduling allows individuals to buffer against interannual variability in food availability while maintaining a steady recruitment contribution over their lifetime.

The early life stages of this grenadier are characterized by traits that enhance survival in the pelagic realm. Egg diameter measurements from ovarian samples average 1.3 millimeters, yielding an estimated wet weight of approximately 0.0012 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0012 grams] at the moment of hatching. This minute mass reflects the high fecundity typical of deep-sea fishes, where large numbers of small offspring are produced to offset elevated larval mortality in the dilute food environment of the open ocean. The yolk-sac larvae rely on endogenous reserves during the first days post-eclosion before transitioning to active feeding on microzooplankton. Growth during this period is slow relative to that of epipelagic species, a pattern consistent with the reduced metabolic demands imposed by the cold temperatures prevailing at depth.

Adults of Nezumia aequalis reach a maximum recorded total length of 36 centimeters [Li = 36 centimeters], making this species one of the larger members of its genus in the western North Atlantic. The corresponding maximum somatic wet weight, estimated from morphometric relationships validated against dissected specimens, approaches 130 grams [Wwi = 130 grams]. These values are derived from bottom-trawl collections spanning the continental slope between 200 and 800 meters depth. Body size in this species shows a pronounced relationship with latitude, with individuals from more northerly grounds tending toward slightly greater lengths, possibly reflecting differences in productivity regimes across its geographic range. The length-weight relationship used to generate these estimates follows a typical allometric scaling for macrourids, with body mass increasing disproportionately relative to length.

Longevity in Nezumia aequalis has been assessed through otolith increment analysis of individuals captured during long-term monitoring programs. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species, based on validated annuli counts, is approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years] under the ambient thermal conditions of its habitat, which consistently average 9.3 °C [T = 9.3 °C]. This extended lifespan, coupled with late maturation and moderate fecundity, positions the species firmly within a slow life-history continuum that is common among deep-water teleosts. Reproductive senescence has not been systematically documented in this species, though the oldest individuals in the sample exhibited reduced gonad mass relative to prime-age adults, suggesting a possible decline in fecundity at advanced ages. The otolith-derived longevity estimate aligns with values reported for other macrourids of comparable body size inhabiting similar thermal regimes along the continental margin.
